nodes.label: Universal Design for Learning Principles
nodes.one_line: Build one lesson that already works for learners who'd otherwise need three separate accommodated versions.
know_what: Three UDL principles — multiple means of representation, action and expression, and engagement (CAST framework)
Means of representation — presenting content through more than one modality (text plus audio plus visual) so no single format is the only access point
Means of action and expression — letting a learner demonstrate mastery through more than one output format (write, speak, build, present)
Means of engagement — varying how content is framed and paced to sustain motivation across learners with different interests and self-regulation needs
UDL vs. accommodation — UDL designs flexibility in from the start; an accommodation retrofits access for one learner after the fact, at higher cost and lower coverage
Curb-cut effect — a UDL feature built for one group, such as captions for deaf learners, that benefits a much wider audience, such as anyone in a loud room
know_how: Check a lesson plan against all three UDL principles and note which ones are currently addressed by only one option
Add a second modality, such as audio narration or a visual diagram, to content that currently exists in only one format
Offer at least two ways for a learner to demonstrate mastery of an objective where the objective itself doesn't require a specific format
Build optional scaffolds, such as a glossary or background primer, into the design rather than distributing them only to learners who ask
Identify a planned accommodation that could instead be built in as a default option for everyone
Review captions, alt text, and color contrast against WCAG guidelines as part of the UDL pass, not a separate compliance step
habits: Ask what happens if a learner couldn't use this format, about every planned content type
Look for the accommodation that's really a design gap, not an individual exception
Default to offering options over building one 'main' version plus special-case fixes
Check representation, expression, and engagement separately — a design can nail one and miss the other two
Treat accessibility review as part of the design pass, not a QA step tacked on at the end
nodes.checkpoint: Redesign one existing lesson against all three UDL principles, adding at least one new representation option, one new expression option, and one new engagement option, without changing the underlying objective.
nodes.common_failure: Treating UDL as an accessibility add-on applied late to one 'main' version of a course, instead of a design principle that shapes the format choices from the first draft.
sources: CAST, Universal Design for Learning Guidelines
Thomas Tobin & Kirsten Behling, Reach Everyone, Teach Everyone

nodes.label: Worked Example Design
nodes.one_line: Show a fully solved problem in a way that reduces a novice's cognitive load instead of just modeling the answer.
know_what: Worked example — a fully solved problem showing every step, studied instead of attempted, to reduce a novice's extraneous cognitive load
Worked-example effect — the finding (Sweller, Cooper) that studying worked examples produces better novice learning outcomes than solving equivalent problems unaided
Faded worked example — a sequence moving from fully worked to partially worked to unaided, gradually transferring the cognitive work to the learner
Self-explanation prompt — a question embedded in a worked example asking the learner to justify a step, which increases engagement without adding search load
Near vs. far transfer example — a worked example matched closely to the target task versus one requiring further generalization, chosen based on how much transfer the objective needs
Split-attention effect — a design flaw where a worked example's text and diagram are physically or temporally separated, forcing the learner to hold one in memory while finding the other
know_how: Write out a fully worked example for a target task, showing every intermediate step an expert would otherwise skip
Build a faded sequence of three to four examples moving from fully worked to blank practice
Insert self-explanation prompts at key decision steps instead of just presenting the solution silently
Integrate text and diagram physically, with labels on the diagram itself instead of a separate legend, to avoid the split-attention effect
Choose near-transfer examples for procedural objectives and a mix of near and far examples for objectives requiring generalization
Pilot a worked example with a genuine novice and watch where their attention gets lost, not just whether they get the right answer
habits: Write the full expert solution first, then decide what to fade and what to keep
Check a worked example for split attention by looking at it as a first-time novice would
Ask whether a step that seems obvious to an expert actually needs to be shown
Build the fade sequence deliberately instead of jumping straight from fully worked to unaided practice
Watch a real novice work through the example before assuming it's clear
nodes.checkpoint: Design a three-step faded worked-example sequence for one procedural objective, with self-explanation prompts and no split-attention layout, and pilot it with one genuine novice.
nodes.common_failure: Jumping straight from a single worked example to unaided practice, skipping the faded intermediate steps that actually transfer the cognitive work to the learner gradually.
sources: John Sweller & Graham Cooper, the worked-example effect
Alexander Renkl, learning from worked examples and self-explanation

nodes.label: Scaffolding & Fading
nodes.one_line: Support a learner just enough to succeed at a task they couldn't do alone yet, then remove the support on a plan, not a whim.
know_what: Scaffolding — temporary support that lets a learner succeed at a task above their current independent ability, calibrated to be removable
Zone of proximal development (Vygotsky) — the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with support, which scaffolding is designed to occupy
Fading — the planned, gradual withdrawal of scaffolding as competence increases, distinct from support that never gets removed
Types of scaffold — procedural (checklists, sentence starters), conceptual (concept maps, worked models), strategic (prompts for planning or self-monitoring), metacognitive (reflection prompts)
Scaffold overuse — support that remains past the point the learner needs it, which can suppress the independent performance a course is trying to build
Contingent support — adjusting the amount of scaffolding in real time based on how the specific learner is actually performing, rather than a fixed schedule for everyone
know_how: Identify a task just above the learner's current independent ability and design a scaffold specifically for that gap, not a generic aid
Choose a scaffold type — procedural, conceptual, strategic, or metacognitive — matched to what's actually blocking the learner
Plan a fading schedule across a course, specifying when each scaffold gets reduced or removed, before the course launches
Build in a checkpoint to confirm a learner is ready for a scaffold to fade, instead of fading on a fixed calendar regardless of readiness
Watch for scaffold overuse in a pilot — a learner who still needs support at a point the plan assumed independence
Differentiate fading pace for different learners when the format allows it, rather than applying one fixed schedule to everyone
habits: Ask what specific gap a scaffold is closing before adding it
Plan the removal of a scaffold at the same time it's designed, not as an afterthought
Watch for a scaffold that's become a permanent crutch instead of a temporary support
Check whether a struggling learner needs a scaffold added or an earlier scaffold that faded too soon
Differentiate fading pace across learners when the format allows it, rather than assuming uniform readiness
nodes.checkpoint: Design a scaffolded task with a named scaffold type and a written fading schedule across three practice attempts, plus a readiness checkpoint before each fade.
nodes.common_failure: Adding a support, such as a job aid, hint, or template, that helps in the moment but never gets removed, so the course produces learners who can only perform with the aid still in hand.
sources: Lev Vygotsky, zone of proximal development
Wood, Bruner & Ross, the original scaffolding concept
Roy Pea, the social and technical dimensions of scaffolding

nodes.label: Sequencing & Chunking
nodes.one_line: Break content into pieces sized to working memory and order them so each piece leans on the last.
know_what: Chunking — grouping related content into units sized to working memory, commonly cited around four plus or minus items, instead of one continuous stream
Micro-sequencing — the order of steps within a single chunk, distinct from macro-sequencing, the order of chunks across a whole course
Simple-to-complex sequencing — starting with the simplest whole version of a task and adding complexity, rather than teaching isolated sub-skills first
Spiral sequencing — revisiting a concept at increasing depth across a course, instead of covering it once and moving on
Elaboration theory (Reigeluth) — sequencing from a simplified 'epitome' of the whole task toward full complexity, in deliberate elaborative passes
Pacing signal — a design cue, such as a progress indicator or estimated time, that tells a learner where a chunk boundary is, reducing the cognitive cost of not knowing how much is left
know_how: Break a long content stream into chunks sized to a working-memory limit, checking against the audience's actual novice or expert level
Sequence chunks by dependency order established in the prerequisite map, not by convenience of the source material
Apply simple-to-complex sequencing to a skill-based unit by teaching a simplified whole version of the task before isolated sub-skills
Build a spiral revisit of a foundational concept later in the course at greater depth, instead of assuming one pass is sufficient
Mark chunk boundaries visibly in the delivered format, using headings, progress markers, or natural stopping points
Check total chunk count against the audience's realistic attention span for the delivery format, such as a webinar versus a self-paced module
habits: Count how many new elements a single chunk introduces before finalizing it
Ask whether a sequence teaches the whole task simplified first, or isolated parts with no whole in sight until the end
Mark a natural stopping point in every chunk instead of letting content run continuously
Revisit an early foundational concept later at more depth instead of assuming one exposure is enough
Check total chunk count against the audience's realistic attention span for the format
nodes.checkpoint: Break a piece of dense source content into chunks sized to working memory, sequence them by dependency order rather than source order, and mark a visible boundary between chunks.
nodes.common_failure: Chunking by convenient section breaks in the source material instead of by working-memory load and dependency, producing chunks that are still too dense or in the wrong order.
sources: George Miller, 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two'

nodes.label: Active Learning Activity Design
nodes.one_line: Design an activity that makes a learner do the cognitive work the objective actually requires, not just read about it.
know_what: Generative activity — a task requiring the learner to produce something, such as an explanation, a solution, or a summary, rather than passively receive it
Retrieval practice — an activity requiring recall from memory rather than recognition from a provided list, which produces stronger retention than re-reading
Desirable difficulty (Bjork) — a level of challenge that slows performance in the moment but improves long-term retention, distinct from difficulty that just causes frustration
Productive failure — a designed sequence where learners attempt a problem before instruction and fail productively, which can deepen later understanding for some objective types

Fidelity — how closely a practice activity resembles the real-world performance context, and the tradeoff between higher fidelity (more realistic, more expensive) and lower fidelity (cheaper, faster to iterate)
Passive-activity trap — an activity that looks interactive, such as clicking a hotspot or dragging a label, but requires no real cognitive work matching the objective
know_how: Design an activity requiring the learner to generate an answer, explanation, or artifact instead of just selecting or reading one
Build in retrieval practice, recall without notes, at spaced intervals instead of relying only on initial exposure
Calibrate difficulty to be desirably hard — enough friction to require real effort, not so much that most learners fail outright
Match activity fidelity to the objective's real-world stakes, using lower-fidelity practice early and higher-fidelity practice closer to the terminal objective
Audit a planned activity by asking what cognitive operation it actually requires, catching passive-activity-trap designs before build
Pilot a new activity type with a small group and check whether they engage with the intended cognitive work or route around it
habits: Ask what the learner is actually doing mentally about every planned activity, not just what they're clicking
Prefer an activity that requires recall over one that only requires recognition
Notice when an interactive-looking activity is actually passive underneath
Check whether an activity's difficulty is productive or just frustrating
Match activity fidelity to how close the course is to the terminal objective

know_why.claim: Practice activities should require retrieval from memory rather than recognition from provided options wherever the objective allows it.
know_why.because: retrieval practice produces measurably stronger long-term retention than restudying or recognition-based review, even though it feels harder and slower in the moment
know_why.disputed_by: some rapid-development and engagement-focused practitioners who favor lower-friction recognition-based interactions, such as drag-and-drop or click-reveal, because they're faster to build and score better on immediate learner-satisfaction surveys
know_why.source: Roediger & Karpicke, the testing effect / retrieval practice research, vs. common e-learning engagement-metric practice

nodes.checkpoint: Design one activity per objective in a module that requires generative retrieval rather than recognition, with a stated fidelity level matched to the objective's real-world stakes.
nodes.common_failure: Building an activity that's visually interactive, such as drag-and-drop or click-to-reveal, but cognitively equivalent to passive reading, so learners complete it without doing the mental work the objective requires.
sources: Henry Roediger & Jeffrey Karpicke, the testing effect

nodes.label: Course Blueprint Assembly
nodes.one_line: Produce the single document that specifies every module, activity, and assessment well enough that someone else could build from it.
know_what: Course blueprint / design document — the single artifact specifying every module's objectives, strategy, activities, assessments, and duration, ready for a build team to work from
Design document vs. storyboard — the blueprint specifies the plan at the module level; a storyboard specifies it at the screen level for production
Traceability matrix — a section of the blueprint explicitly linking every objective to its assessment and its primary activity, so nothing gets lost between planning and build
Sign-off gate — a defined point where the sponsor and SME approve the blueprint before production spend begins, protecting against late-stage redesign
Level of detail calibration — a blueprint detailed enough to guide a build team without being so exhaustive it becomes a second full draft of the course
Change control — the process for handling a requested change after blueprint sign-off, distinguishing a small clarification from a scope change requiring re-approval
know_how: Assemble a single document specifying every module's objectives, chosen instructional strategy, activities, assessments, and estimated duration
Build a traceability matrix linking every objective to its assessment and primary activity within the blueprint
Route the blueprint through a formal sign-off gate with the sponsor and SME before authorizing production spend
Calibrate the blueprint's level of detail to guide the build team without duplicating the eventual storyboard
Set up a change-control process distinguishing a minor clarification from a scope change that needs re-approval
Cross-check the blueprint against the curriculum map to confirm this module still fits the larger program without new redundancy or gaps
habits: Check every objective in the blueprint has both an assessment and an activity before calling it done
Get sign-off in writing before authorizing any production spend against the blueprint
Ask whether a requested change is a clarification or a scope change before agreeing to it informally
Keep the blueprint at planning-level detail and resist the pull to turn it into a screen-by-screen storyboard
Cross-check the blueprint against the curriculum map before calling a module finished
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a signed-off course blueprint for one module with a complete traceability matrix linking every objective to an assessment and an activity, and a documented change-control process.
nodes.common_failure: Starting production before the blueprint is signed off, so a late objective change forces already-built material to be reworked or discarded.
sources: Michael Allen, Leaving ADDIE for SAM
Cathy Moore, Action Mapping design document format
